newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina hopes "no surprises" after Brazil deal.
newsitem.headline: Argentina hopes "no surprises" after Brazil deal.

text.p: Argentina hopes there will be no new scares among Mercosur partners after the trade bloc patched up a dispute with Brazil over new import finance rules, Deputy Foreign Minister Andres Cisneros said Thursday.
"We have agreed to coordinate macroeconomic measures so that there will be no more surprises because of measures taken by sovereign countries," he told local radio.
Brazil infuriated its Mercosur partners Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay last week with new limits on import financing of less than 360 days, effectively forcing importers to pay cash.
But after a chorus of complaints of "protectionism", they struck a deal Wednesday agreeing changes to the rules for Mercosur for 120 days while a long-term solution is sought.
Brazil's Mercosur partners were angry it did not consult them before taking action to head off its growing trade gap.

"Countries who participate in an integration process have their sovereignty restricted," said Cisneros, adding that new macroeconomic measures that could affect trading partners must be "reported to and debated with the other member countries."

Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez and Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan thrashed out a deal under which Brazil agreed to two rule changes for Mercosur -- altering the definition of "paying cash" to exempt more products, and raising to $40,000 from $10,000 the upper limit for exemption.
But Cisneros, who took part in the talks, said: "This is neither a win for Argentina nor a retreat for Brazil."

Fernandez told reporters in Brazil that Argentine industry had exaggerated the "catastrophic" consequences Brazil's move could have on their exports. Argentina had a $1.0 billion trade surplus with Brazil last year, exporting $6.5 billion of goods to its giant northern neighbor.
Enrique Mantilla, head of the Argentine Exporters' Chamber, told reporters Thursday that the deal had ended a crisis which threatened Mercosur's credibility.

"We still need to know the fine print of the new rules issued by the Brazilian Central Bank, but the main thing is to use these 120 days to negotiate a framework giving more space to businesses," he said.
